implementation_notes: Go has no inheritance and no null-safe reference type: the collaborator is an interface, the null object is a type whose methods do nothing, and the standard library ships the canonical ones - io.Discard is 'a Writer on which all Write calls succeed without doing anything', io.NopCloser supplies a no-op Close, and since Go 1.24 slog.DiscardHandler 'discards all log output' with Enabled returning false for every level. Because calling a nil interface panics, the pattern is usually applied at construction: a nopLogger or io.Discard fallback is substituted in the constructor (if l == nil { l = NopLogger }), so the rest of the code calls unconditionally. Where absence is an error, prefer returning (T, error) and checking err instead.
pitfalls: A nil interface and an interface holding a nil pointer differ: l == nil is false for a typed-nil *myLogger, so the fallback silently misses and the call panics on a nil receiver - check the concrete value or avoid nullable constructor parameters.
io.Discard has fast paths that a wrapping writer loses, and slog.DiscardHandler is a writable package variable; treat both as shared but do not assume another package cannot replace the handler.
The zero value is not a null object: a zero slog.Logger is unusable and a slog.Logger built with a nil handler panics, so use the shipped discard implementations instead of zero-value structs.
